name: Pomatum

lead: Pomatum is a greasy, often perfumed hair dressing made from animal fat or later petroleum-based and waxy ingredients. It slicks, shines and sculpts hair, making styles such as the pompadour, quiff and ducktail possible.

The name comes from the Medieval Latin form of the word pomade, from French pommade and Italian pomata. Pomades were more popular in the 1920s-50s, and returned in the 2010s with undercuts and slicked styles.

paras: A small amount is worked through the hair and combed or sculpted into shape. Oil-based pomades range from light hold with a wet shine to heavy waxy holds; water-based versions wash out more easily.

Heavy, petroleum-based products are associated by some in the hair-care world with buildup, clogged follicles and irritation, driving a shift to natural-ingredient formulas. Fragranced products can cause reactions in sensitive people.

angle.text: Pomatum gives immediate hold and gloss, letting wearers sculpt styles like the pompadour or quiff. The effect lasts until the hair is washed.

lead: Pomatum is the older name for pomade, a greasy or waxy substance used to style hair [1]. It gives hair shine, hold and a groomed finish, and is what makes sculpted, swept-back styles possible.

Pomades of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries were mainly bear fat or lard, often scented; by the early twentieth century petroleum jelly, beeswax and lard were common, and lanolin and beeswax were used extensively later [1]. The word derives from the Medieval Latin pomatum, and French pommade and Italian pomata, from the word for apple, because mashed apples were sometimes added for scent [1].

paras: Pomatum, or pomade, is a greasy, waxy or water-based styling product. Fat was also used to capture and preserve the scent of flowers, and "pomade" can mean a wax extract of fragrant flowers [1].

The article on pomade notes that ancient Egyptians used animal-fat products on hair and wigs. Named brands include Morgan's Pomade (UK, 1873), Murray's Superior Pomade (1925), Sweet Georgia Brown (1934) and Royal Crown (1936), and Dixie Peach was popular with American teenage boys from World War II into the 1960s [1].
Use declined after the 1950s; the pompadour was a cultural phenomenon from the mid-1950s to 1964. Pomade returned in the 2010s, partly because the disconnected undercut suits heavy-hold products [1].

Oil-based pomades are graded heavy, medium or light hold; heavier products have more wax and less shine, while light brilliantines have more oil and a wet look. Water-based gels and "unorthodox" water-based pomades wash out more easily [1].
Concerns about buildup, clogged follicles and irritation from petroleum-based products have driven demand for natural formulas using shea butter, beeswax and plant oils [1].
